en: He was a soul grown exceedingly old;
Your gray-maned uncle Bakai
Had reached a great age.
Facing death,
He had grown too feeble even to crawl.
It was his destined hour;
Alas, your uncle Bakai
Had been overtaken by old age.
His raven-dark eyes were bloodshot,
His beard beneath his chin had whitened:
It was his hour to die!
No second one will come into the world;
Your forefather, old Bakai,
Will never return or be found again.
He was noble, he was a lion,
His fortune was complete;
The Creator will never again
Create a soul like Bakai.
The people wailed and the nation grieved,
They stood engulfed in clamor;
Unmatched among true men,
He stood amid the tumult.
If only the thoroughbred never tired,
If only frail man never aged,
If only the wide world never narrowed,
And each might live as he desired;
If only the mighty, boundless Creator
Would let all remain in its proper course,
I would have no regret—
If only it were so.
A man observes this and reflects,
Shaking his head and crying, “Alas!”
His body went slack as night descended,
And he turned his face toward death.
“Alas, he has fallen beyond recovery,” they said;
“This cruel, faithless, lying world!
Our mighty father Bakai
Has come to nothing,” they said.
“The teeth with which he ate his food
Have fallen out,” they said.
“The strength that kindled fire in both hands
Has left him,” they said.
“His feet that bore him
Down the slopes,
Alas, brave heart, have failed,” they said.
“The dreadful curse of affliction
Has wholly consumed him,” they said.
The season of courage and valor
Had passed away like this.
When old age came upon him,
The gray-maned hero Bakai
Had no flesh left, only bone,
Scarcely a spoonful of blood beneath his chin—
A creature reduced to crawling.
In your prime, splendid in sable,
You used to wear it proudly;
When black night fell upon the Kyrgyz,
You plunged into the clash.
Overcoming all who grappled with you,
How many peoples we used to rout!
His fortune was complete,
He was a lion upheld by the spirits;
While ancestral power and honor remain,
A man never truly dies.
He gathered the wealth of the world;
Across the whole universe
He sought ancestral lands—
Bakai was a lion among heroes.
Clad in blue lynx fur,
Bearing a blue-mottled shield,
He blinded those he marked
And ruled the whole world.
No enemy reached his frontier,
Nor did he live off the treasury.
Great was your dignity, fierce your wrath,
Alas, our forefather Bakai.
One day is light and one day night—
This accursed, fleeting world:
Behold how false it is,
How it parts one from one’s companion
And leaves one behind.
His beard had whitened like a swan;
When the day of his journey came,
Behold how he was parted
From Manas, his companion in time.
Behold how it heaped
Toil and misery upon his head.
What is seen today is gone tomorrow;
This accursed world is filth—
Behold how false it is.
Behold how the golden throne
On which he sat slipped away.
Behold how he was parted
From the fortune in his hands.
Though wishing to die, he could not die,
Nor could he take his own life;
Along the road of death and fate
He could not walk by himself.
He could not lay his noble head,
Still living, in the grave.
Stripped of his fortune,
Parted from his peers,
His time had come to waste away,
To tear at
And pluck out this beard.
To the race he once would enter,
His time had come not to go.
Though nearing the true world,
His time had come when he could do nothing.
Parted from his pacing steed,
His time had come to trudge on foot.
Parted from his imposing presence,
His time had come to be pitied.
His sable cap became mere dust,
His suffering became idle gossip:
His time had come to decline.
Though Bakai was eighty,
He still had deeds he could perform,
And a road leading to Judgment Day;
He still had wondrous words to speak.
Though mortal, his true self remained;
If you took Bakai’s measure,
His speech was as it had been before.
Heard throughout the universe,
My father Bakai possessed great renown.
When he was born into the world,
He came alone, yet was worth a nation.
His eyes saw from afar,
His heart was utterly clear—
Gray-maned Bakai was a sage.
From amid a vast assembly,
He emerged alone to win the race.
As the people bowed and made way,
Their hearts divided in countless thoughts.
Behold old Bakai:
His resolute heart was torn,
Tears poured from his eyes;
Facing what had befallen him,
He raised his hands and cried, “God!
Oh, my son Seytek, my tiger,
Oh, for your black eyes, bright as glass,
Oh, my cuckoo left behind,
Let me cherish you!
On the mountain ridge you are a bloodthirsty eagle,
A champion left as our living sign;
You are a spring flowing since ancient times,
A champion left to inherit our legacy.
While the people wail and the nation cries out,
Thus do we hold your celebration;
For your life, my foal,
We keep praying to God!
For every flutter of your eyelashes,
My son, we keep praying to God.
Seeing you brings peace to the heart;
When we look upon you, no grief remains.
My plane tree risen on barren ground,
Whose shade shelters and sustains the people!
My black-browed falcon,
Who catches wild geese without a hood,
At whose soaring my soul rejoices,
My falcon unerring when he takes aim,
My racehorse at the tether,
Who wins the prize without cooling down,
My foals Kuyaly and Seytek,
My gyrfalcon who drove
The croaking ravens
Back into their proper place!
My poor dear ones, for whom I would give my life.
Maiden lion Kuyaly and brave Seytek,
My matched pair of plane trees,
Now that my beard is white as a swan
And the hour of my journey draws near,
I pray that He preserve you both—
This I ask of the Almighty!
My matched pair of lions,
You who tirelessly wage battle,
You have delivered a sorrowing nation
From its torment.
You are the figure before my eyes,
The presence on whom I rely;
My finger’s breadth when I measure,
My cherished descendants
Who sit beside me.
Ancestors and children, amen!
May your embers turn to gold;
May your life be long!
May the throne you mount be golden;
Amen, may God favor you!
May fortune settle upon your brow.
My son Seytek, hear me:
If you observe me, I hold mystery within;
I am a soul of Lokman the Wise,
I am great old Bakai,
I am the giver of blessings.
I made the withered grow green,
I made the aged young again,
I made the pale bloom with life;
Whoever prospered when I spread my palms,
Whoever heard me spread my hands and say, ‘Amen,’
Found happiness.
My blessings never went astray;
A curse I uttered in wrath
Never took more than six days.
There is gold within my words,
And every wonder dwells within me.
His spoken word became proclamation:
No less than a prophet
Was King Bakai, the elder;
He was himself a saint,
He was the discerning eye of wisdom.
Spreading his hands and saying, “Amen,”
Our mighty forefather Bakai
Bestowed his righteous blessing—
The wellspring of the world beyond,
My mighty, far-seeing uncle,
Bestowed his great blessing.
A blessing to unite the people,
A blessing that would take effect,
A blessing that would stand unwavering
Until Judgment Day.
Ready as a sparrowhawk,
Into Khan Bakai’s mouth
Wisdom came from the unseen.
Such was King Bakai,
Fruit of the warm earth,
Bearing meaning upon his brow,
The citadel of a sovereign nation.
You became the gateway of the city,
The worthiest among men.
Speaking softly, yet striking firmly,
Noble old Bakai
Opened a mine of countless riches:
His speech was sugar, his words had power,
Yet such a soul now falters.
Bakai gave his blessing:
“May you keep a royal court and become khan,
And be a saintly soul,
Splitting a black hair with perfect judgment,
A man of utter fairness.
May your enemy’s path grow narrow;
When you grapple with the foe,
May the spirit of your father Manas
Be your companion and protector!
May the Forty Saints accompany you against the foe,
And may Khidr come at your cry.
May Bak-Baabedin strike in wrath;
May unity, abundance, and sacred grace,
My son, descend upon you!
Oh, amen, my son, amen!
May the milk of every yielding udder flow;
When you reach for your desire,
May the enemy you face be subdued,
And may your brow open brightly like a flower!
When you journey far,
When you enter battle,
May Zhol-Baabedin accompany you!
